Fires in mid-September burned 30 to 40 kilometers (19 to 25 miles) from the perimeter of government buildings. cards.source_text: The more power the radical rightwing nationalists of our age accrue, the greater the risk that their destructive brand of politics becomes normalised. We should not, for instance, regard it as normal that the man in charge of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals casually promises “a whole civilisation will die tonight”. We should not accept that history’s first trillionaire is allowed to spread racist conspiracy theories to a hitherto unimaginable extent. We should be alarmed that, here in the UK, a party tipped to lead a potential future government is trying to cruise to power in the slipstream of this international movement. In fact, we shouldn’t just be alarmed by such developments: we should stop them and urgently repair the damage already done. But how? And what is the nature of that damage? This bold, clarifying intervention from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor provides some of the answers. “End times fascism” is their term for a convergence of interests that can broadly be understood as a response to the climate crisis. Faced with a world coming under unprecedented strain from environmental shocks and an unequal, resource-hungry economic system, today’s reactionaries are effectively saying: bring it on. “The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating,” Klein and Taylor write, describing a loose alliance of three principal factions rooted in US political and business elites. First are the religious fanatics who see each new disaster as a welcome sign we are entering the end of days, but find common ground with secular demagogues who promise a glorious, prosperous future on the ruins of our present. Think, for instance, of the mirage of a “New Gaza”, a property developers’ fever dream that the Trump administration – heavily influenced by Christian Zionists – claims will arise from the wreckage of Israel’s US-backed genocide. Next are the new tech barons, who preach that only the AI “arms race”, as Klein and Taylor put it, can save humanity – even as its demand for water and electricity scorches the planet – while they themselves dream of sitting out societal breakdown in remote, fortified enclaves. Last come the political entrepreneurs who transform visions of disaster into votes by promising to turn their nations into bunkered garrison states. cards.source_text: China Miéville’s epic new novel is presented as being “20 years in the making”. It is quite a testament to how extravagant – even Stakhanovite – his imagination is that during that period he also produced six novels (including The City & the City and The Book of Elsewhere, co-written with Keanu Reeves), two novellas, two series of graphic novels, a children’s book, a volume of short stories and two works of nonfiction, on the October Revolution and the Communist Manifesto. It does not mean that these works were, as Graham Greene called The Third Man and Our Man in Havana, “entertainments” – Embassytown, to my mind, is the best translation of deconstructionist philosophy into science fiction – but certainly The Rouse is a quantum jump in terms of ambition, moral seriousness and stylistic bravado. It means that rather than classifying Miéville with “the new weird” or “speculative fantasy”, he ought to be compared to Roberto Bolaño or Mircea Cărtărescu. This new novel is equally maximalist, dense, disorienting and discomfiting, reflecting how surreal our reality seems to have become. Readers acquainted with Miéville’s other work might be disconcerted by the first hundred pages: broadly speaking, they are social realism. We are in 1970s London and Maur, short for Maureen, gets pregnant and decides to keep the baby. Ewan grows up reading Rupert Bear and Starlord comics, watching Steptoe and Son and Rentaghost, and having Chinese takeaways with obligatory background racism. It is canny rather than uncanny, with the exception of a cameo from the truly odd 80s comedian Roy Jay doing his “slither-spook” routine, possibly on The Bob Monkhouse Show. (Now an internet meme, it is unforgettable and queasily sinister – and on YouTube.) Eventually Ewan, at a loss in many ways, decides to join the army. Then Miéville drops the bombshell just before the 100th page: Ewan dies, supposedly by suicide, at an army base. “Now everything is codas,” thinks Maur, and in capital letters we get THE END. The novel – all epilogue – now begins, for more than a thousand pages. cards.source_text: The most interesting chapter in Anthony Scaramucci’s All the Wrong Moves is the one where the hedge funder turned podcaster goes to work for Donald Trump. It’s summer 2017, and he’s been given the job of comms director, which he doesn’t know how to do, but he and Trump think it’ll work out because they’re both from New York. Or maybe he took it because he had “Potomac fever”, which afflicts Wall Street financiers who find themselves on the riverfront in Washington DC thinking they know how to run a country just because they’re “full of power and judgmental insight … about to fix everything”. This appointment lasts only 11 days, not even enough time to be truly tainted by Trump’s first term, though it is enough time for Scaramucci to miss the birth of his son. The account is a mea culpa soup, with the author full of regrets for his hubris, his impulsivity, his “pride, egotism and asinine stupidity”, the fact that, despite the clear-sightedness bestowed by his humble beginnings, he’d come to assume the collective biases of the rich people he hung out with. But what he doesn’t address is the fact that it was quite plain by then who Donald Trump was. Scaramucci himself identifies the beginning of Trump’s explicit use of racism and the politics of hatred, not in his first taboo-breaking statement that Mexicans were bringing drugs and rapists into the US (2015), but with the Obama birther conspiracy, which had been going on for years. Irrespective of all his pondering as to whether Trump was symptom or cause of a broken US, Scaramucci knew when he joined the White House that he was reporting to a racist, a chancer, an egomaniac and a liar. Bluntly, a person with decent values would not have joined this administration. That doesn’t invalidate his analysis, but it does flatten it. The US is all about money, he tells us; the founding fathers were actually the investing fathers; anything not obviously a decision motivated by money is the unintended consequence of one. The very United States was “unified – by money”, because that was all Alexander Hamilton was thinking when he created a central bank. The fact that half the English-speaking world could sing the thousand other things Hamilton was thinking in a close harmony hasn’t occurred to the author, who can’t have seen the musical. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 19 minute listen I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue. This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media. Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information. Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. cards.source_text: ‘What do you think this movie is about?’ In this video essay, the US filmmaker Kevin B Lee recalls the shock of seeing, as a young film buff, the raw, violent and widely acclaimed Vietnam War film Platoon (1986) with his family in a San Francisco cinema. Recording outside the building that once housed that cinema, he details his harrowing time in the theatre and the film’s reverberations in his life beyond the theatre’s walls, including how it stirred generational trauma in his family and racism at school. With his deceptively simple approach, Lee inverts and subverts Oliver Stone’s epic, crafting, on a shoestring budget, a profound and intensely personal meditation on memory. Lee’s video essay was published as part of ‘Once Upon a Screen’, a series of video essays about film viewing and childhood trauma, commissioned and curated by Ariel Avissar and Evelyn Kreutzer, for The Cine-Files journal of cinema studies, Issue 15.

cards.source_text: When he was a child growing up in Emilia-Romagna, my great-grandfather Marco once found an eagle fledgling that had fallen from its nest. He kept it warm in the folds of his shirt and ran home, only to discover as he undressed that the bird had eaten strips of his flesh, its beak tinged red with blood. The rescued eagle thrived in my great-grandfather’s care, its wingspan soon a remarkable length. And all the while, Marco himself grew immensely tall. Then, one day, without warning, the eagle flew away. The moment my father told me this story when I was a boy, it lodged itself deep in my imagination. I pictured young Marco as a giant striding through the forests of north-central Italy, calling to the bird of prey, waiting in vain for it to land on his outstretched hand. Marco merged with the heroes of my illustrated classical civilisation books, earning his place between the busts of Roman emperors and the chapters on Greek mythology. What I never realised was that this family legend held clues to who I am and to my relationship to Italy. Lina Stores deli in Soho, London, has been a pillar of Italian life in England for decades. It’s where we’d sometimes meet our paternal grandparents when visiting London from our home in France. My brothers and I would line up in front of the refrigerated counter and ask for our favourite ravioli, doing our utmost to avoid any slip-ups in Italian that would make the staff wince: ‘ricotta e spinaci’, ‘zucca’, ‘funghi porcini’. Back at our grandparents’ flat, Nonna served the ravioli on an elaborately laid table, and my grandfather appeared with freshly grated Parmigiano. He’d sprinkle the cheese evenly over our pasta; never too much, nor too little. How he did this, and with such speed, we didn’t know. If we had spaghetti, Nonna would wrap her right hand around ours and twirl the fork with us so we held just the right amount, the bespattered tablecloth damning proof of our slapdash habits at home. My grandparents trusted that these rituals of the table (they saw them as basic codes of Italianness, connecting displaced Italians everywhere) would allow us to paper over the differences in our ethnically blended and peripatetic family. In this way, we’d be able to claim Italian identity for ourselves, despite its competition in our lives with Englishness and Frenchness. cards.source_text: The ancient craft of hedge laying is experiencing a strong revival as farmers use techniques that peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries to boost wildlife, capture carbon and help tackle flooding. Hedge laying, which restores and revives mature hedges to keep them fresh, was among the four most popular categories of capital grants selected by farmers out of a total pot of £225m provided by the government this year to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside. The 2,500 farmers across England who applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using a craft that dates back thousands of years, will – if the grants are approved – lay 1,300km (800 miles) of mature hedgerows, enough to stretch from Land’s End to Hadrian’s Wall and back. Megan Gimber, the key habitats officer for the People’s Trust for Endangered Species, said hedge laying was one of the most effective tools farmers had to respond to the climate crisis. “Hedge laying really stopped after the war, so it has been over a generation since it was a normal part of farm management and we have seen a huge decline in hedgerows as a result,” she said. “These grants will give 1,300km of potentially ancient hedges a new lease of life, to help plug the gap, and it is fantastic that it is such a popular grant application.” Mature, maintained hedgerows are a carbon sink, capturing more carbon in every hectare than forests. They support thousands of species, provide shade for livestock, reduce soil erosion and slow down, absorb and store vast amounts of rainwater to help reduce flooding. “They are massively important,” said Stephen Budding, the chair of the National Hedgelaying Society. “The greatest biodiversity gain is from hedge laying older hedges. “Our members are seeing quite a surge in work, but I don’t think this would be happening without the government grants available.” Hedge laying involves cutting through the hedge stems almost completely, then laying them at an angle to the ground. Laying the branches down invigorates growth at the point where they have been cut, filling gaps in the hedges and restoring youth and freshness. It is done by hand by skilled layers – many of whom will compete next month at the National Hedgelaying Championships in Chipping Norton. cards.source_text: Dawn has broken, and the air is cool and still. It’s at about this time that gibbons usually erupt into song, wa-oo-ing and wa-ing from the highest branches and filling the tree tops with rich melodies. But in this corner of Malaysian forest, bordered by housing and roads, the resident white-handed gibbons are quiet. All that can be heard is the hum of traffic from a nearby highway. This isn’t a rare occurrence for this group of gibbons, according to research, which found these particular gibbons, named Mambang and Walinong, appeared to be producing far fewer morning songs than others that are not exposed to the same level of traffic noise. White-handed gibbons, arboreal animals whose calls can travel more than half a mile through dense forest canopies, are known for their complex songs and vocal techniques that have been likened to those of soprano singers. But as their habitats are increasingly fragmented by roads, industry and urban development, researchers say there is a growing need to understand how human-generated noise is affecting when and how they sing. “Their songs are not just background noise or a way of announcing their presence. They play an important role in communication between groups, territorial interactions and social relationships,” says Nadine Ruppert, associate professor at Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a supervisor of the research. “So when we introduce persistent human-generated noise into their habitat, we are potentially interfering with a very important part of their lives,” she says. In 2023 and 2024, for a week in both wet and dry seasons, Benjamin Galea, a final-year PhD student at Universiti Sains Malaysia, and the author of the study, recorded and analysed the morning calls of white-handed gibbons living in three different locations that had varying levels of background noise. They included the spot near the highway, which had the highest level of continual noise pollution, a popular hiking trail, and a secluded beachfront location that was the furthest from human activity. Galea’s research, which is yet to be peer reviewed, found that the greater the background noise, the less likely gibbons were to call. cards.source_text: Stands of tufted hair-grass, some over a metre tall, burned beige by the summer heat, were churned by strong autumn westerlies. Over and through the vegetation’s swaying lather roved a flock of about 200 goldfinches, most of them this year’s young. They were intent on the hanks of thistle and knapweed seed which lay below the hair-grass “canopy”. These immature finches lack any of the red and black bands of the adult’s head. Instead of the smooth mocha buff on their parents’ underparts, the youngsters were dull and streaky. What they had to perfection were the semi-circular disks of yellow across each black wing, while every feather through that full fan was tipped with white. As they moved from place to place, working through the grasses, so the birds created double bands of brightness that shone in intermittent sunlight. The whole scene – the frothing plant stems and the shifting birds – produced exquisite countervailing patterns of movement. An old name for goldfinch is “tailorbird”. It’s said to refer to the white eye-holes inserted into their tail- and wing-tips. As the birds worked away, winnowing thistle floss from seed, letting hanks float off on the breeze, it occurred to me that these prolonged ecological relationships with cottony material could also explain the “tailor” name. It may further account for the birds’ love of spiders’ silk and wool and other fibres as nest material: they are surely tailorbirds in name and nature. As they showered up and descended again in patterns of yellow flecking, it also came to me that the visual impact and the sounds of the flock are more than mere analogues. They seem party to some greater creative whole. Goldfinch calls are soft, tinkling, fragmented, but also somehow molten and blended one to another like melting flakes of gold – no, not gold, but something rarer, something more meaningful than mere metal. Let’s say the dust from some exploded star in a far galaxy that wandered and settled hereabouts 5 billion years ago, only to be infused with something rarest of all: soiled, earthy and – here at Priestcliffe today – called “life”.

cards.source_text: Maybe it’s dumb to be a believer. There’s no guarantee that your beliefs will hold up, and it’s unlikely the thing you reach out for will ever reach back. But to commit to this possibility, as Angela Autumn figures it, is to find connection: to the universe, to other people, or to God if you’re lucky. “I got to be a believer to take a ride,” she sings on the title track of her third studio album, Believer. The people on Autumn’s album have faith in lovers who may not return, in money, in fame, and in nature as a refuge. Autumn herself has had to believe in her songs through an increasingly unstable music economy, moving from a book-your-own-shows independent musician toward a more formal recording career, while also moving further from the sturdy framework of meaning she grew up with. The album is about what belief can engender when certainty is gone, and the possibility of transforming that which is old and battered into something new. No score yet, be the first to add. Autumn grew up Catholic outside Pittsburgh, in the Allegheny region she calls the “Paris of Appalachia.” She was raised around music and nature: Her mother played didgeridoo and made instruments from gourds; her father and family sang together in church. She began playing guitar and banjo at 19, and mainly plays the latter these days, borrowing its open tuning and clawhammer playing style; she also tends to play in an irregular structure indebted to Appalachian music. Influenced by contemporary roots musicians including Rhiannon Giddens, Allison Russell, and Gillian Welch, Autumn eventually moved to Nashville, writing songs that moved between country, indie rock, and grungegrass. cards.source_text: In Before Midnight, the final film in Richard Linklater’s Before Sunrise trilogy, Julie Delpy’s character poses a question to her husband, 20 years after the two fell in love in Vienna: “If we were meeting for the first time today on a train, would you find me attractive?” It’s the kind of existential head-scratcher that makes romance, and its end, infinitely fertile artistic ground. Twenty years and change since many of us fell in love with Bloc Party, the arrival of a new album might have you asking a similar question: If we first encountered them as they are today, would we still fall in love with them? In Linklater’s film, it’s a bittersweet paradox. In this case, it’s a no-brainer: almost certainly not. Even for the Bloc Party faithful, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, framed as the document of a relationship’s dissolution, might prove to be a breakup album in more ways than one. Anatomy of a Brief Romance is Bloc Party’s second breakup album, after 2008’s Intimacy. But this one is more direct, giving us a chronological, blow-by-blow account of an ill-fated couple, one half of which is singer and frontman Kele Okereke. We start with a song named after the day they first locked eyes, “between reps” at the gym (“22.01.22”). We follow them through the dizzying honeymoon period (“Coming On Strong,” “Love Bombs”). We’re there when things get ugly (“Worst Birthday Ever”), and when it all crashes and burns (“Now We Can’t Be Friends,” “Moving On,” “Eulogy”). Okereke’s tale, we’re told, is nothing but the truth. “Every lyric you're hearing on this record was something that actually happened to me,” he says in the press release. “I had to tell the story, from start to finish.” No score yet, be the first to add. What horrors did he endure to inspire this courageous tell-all account? How will his trials and tribulations lend clarity to our own? cards.source_text: For many years, Rio Da Yung OG was—and maybe still is—the most casually hysterical rapper alive. Beginning in 2019, the Flint, Michigan, native rapped with more or less the same flows and the same rhyme schemes on over a dozen projects straight and never grew boring. His humor, at once cartoonishly absurd and ghoulishly authentic, is the type that makes you cup your mouth and hold your breath so you don’t risk laughing over the next punchline. Of all the Michigan street rappers whose hookless strings of devilishly clever non sequiturs lifted the nation’s spirits during lockdown, Rio may be the most consistently entertaining. Between 2021 and 2024, a steady drip of archival material held fans over while Rio served nearly four years of a five-year prison sentence. The music he’s released since being freed has included some of his strongest material yet—but also some of his weakest. On 2025’s remarkably gripping F.L.I.N.T. (Feeling Like I’m Not Through), Rio embodied the album’s title by proving that he had the capacity to evolve beyond his low-stakes shit-talking and paint a more nuanced self-portrait. The gut-busting bars in “Different Music” were solemnly interrupted by Rio’s admission that he cried in prison after losing a string of family and friends. One of his best tracks to date, “Another Story,” was a stream-of-conscious recounting of the larger-than-life traumas he collected throughout his youth. These stray moments of vulnerability only offered brief glimpses at Rio’s psychic wounds, but they added crucial context to his story. The raunchy punchlines hit harder when you know the guy has been through all of that and still has a sense of humor. No score yet, be the first to add. On The World Is Yours, Rio’s clumsy follow-up to the magnificent F.L.I.N.T., the 32-year-old’s signature wit and newfound sensitivity are dampened by a palpable exhaustion that permeates most of the 59-minute affair. cards.source_text: Hakushi Hasegawa believes in the unlimited. Since their earliest releases, the Japanese producer and composer has pursued the dissolution of musical boundaries. They retrofit their tracks with sounds of past and present, covering free jazz and breezy J-rock, even extending to the outer edges of hyperpop’s nebula. Honest Feeling Album, their fourth record, extracts a facsimile of order from the chaos, undergirding the variation with earnest, curious songwriting without smoothing out the gleefully jagged edges. Hasegawa broke out as a teenage wunderkind with their 2018 EP of junglist jazz, Sōmoku hōdō. Subsequent releases stretched to contain more multifarious ideas—their 2019 debut full-length, Air Ni Ni, began to branch out without leaving the Venn diagram of chordally dense jazz and electronic pop, and 2024’s Mahōgakkō was split down the middle, with an anarchic A-side and harmonious B-side. Honest Feeling Album recontextualizes their ever-expanding palette. Rather than relegating genre explorations to different tracks or sides of the record, Hasegawa stuffs every song until they burst. They slalom through the raging noise of “Why the Hell Do I Have to Say Everything From One to Ten Each Time Each Time Each Time Each Time” (featuring half of Otoboke Beaver), the vivacious J-rock of lead single “The Owner of Sweetness,” then back to the wonky TNGHT-esque wubs of “Grace.” The music’s multitudinousness confounds expectations, embracing the disorderly and extraneous. No score yet, be the first to add. Whereas in the past Hasegawa has mostly operated solo, they spend most of Honest Feeling Album as the frontperson and keyboardist of HaHa and the Hairpins, a group of jazz players initially assembled as a backing band for a 2024 live session. The group plays on nearly every track, providing additional energy and dynamism to Hasegawa’s knotty compositions. Kei Matsumaru’s potent sax and Shu Akimoto and Hitomi Aikawa’s percussion are particularly essential to the LP’s freeform jazz current. Akimoto’s skittering drums drive the funk of opener “Little Briar Rose” and Matsumaru’s skronk anchors “The Owner of Sweetness” with a supremely sticky horn hook. cards.source_text: When Sylvan Esso’s self-titled debut dropped in 2014, their electronic songcraft felt novel. It played like a triangulation of Tune-Yards’ digital playground-chants, Everything But the Girl’s soul-folk remixes, and the sing-song indie-pop of Feist, with whom vocalist Amelia Meath toured as backup singer and opener with her woodsy harmony trio Mountain Man. If Sylvan Esso once scanned as a fusion experiment, it now reflects the science of pop, indie or otherwise: idiosyncratic, beat-built, and prone to occasional mea-culpa cultural critiques (an electronic pop tradition from the get-go). What’s always made the group special is Meath’s voice—a bit scuffed, faintly parched but lithe, playful and harmonically on-point, warmly human even when sonically distressed, which it often is. It’s a nice voice to be around, as a listener and, evidently, as an in-demand collaborator: Recently, she’s covered Mazzy Star with Gregory Alan Isakov and Broken Social Scene with Maggie Rogers; she also sung backup on Tyler Childers’ Snipe Hunter and Kevin Morby’s Little Wide Open. No score yet, be the first to add. Ow ∞ is an especially coherent Sylvan Esso album. Unsettled though it is, it boasts a clearer emotional arc than past sets and production that feels particularly fine-tuned, maybe the result of the four-year gap since No Rules Sandy. Per usual, those productions, built with co-pilot Nick Sanborn, give Meath’s voice space to shapeshift and work out its shit, which here seems to involve of-the-moment quandaries: How do you function in a hydrant-flow of current-event horrors? What action do you prioritize? What do you do with the rage? What constitutes self-care? If hedonism counts, when does it become self-abuse? The questions aren’t answered conclusively, but they play out compellingly. And like every Sylvan Esso album, things orbit around a few perfectly-conceived songs. The lead track “Entertainment & Coca-Cola” is an amuse-bouche, its conflicted pledge-of-allegiance to pleasure winking perhaps at Jean-Luc Godard’s famous quote and the carbonated tropicália of Caetano Veloso’s “Alegria, Alegria.” Similarly, the single “Hot Slob” echoes the meta-pop of Sylvan Esso signature “Radio,” but with a different sound—au courant ’90s alt-rock redux with ’70s-glam guitar punctuation. items.summary: Twenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousness China Miéville’s epic new novel is presented as being “20 years in the making”. It is quite a testament to how extravagant – even Stakhanovite – his imagination is that during that period he also produced six novels (including The City & the City and The Book of Elsewhere , co-written with Keanu Reeves), two novellas, two series of graphic novels, a children’s book, a volume of short stories and two works of nonfiction, on the October Revolution and the Communist Manifesto. It does not mean that these works were, as Graham Greene called The Third Man and Our Man in Havana, “entertainments” – Embassytown , to my mind, is the best translation of deconstructionist philosophy into science fiction – but certainly The Rouse is a quantum jump in terms of ambition, moral seriousness and stylistic bravado. It means that rather than classifying Miéville with “the new weird” or “speculative fantasy”, he ought to be compared to Roberto Bolaño or Mircea Cărtărescu. items.summary: The president’s former press secretary has learned all the right lessons, but how come it took him so long? The most interesting chapter in Anthony Scaramucci’s All the Wrong Moves is the one where the hedge funder turned podcaster goes to work for Donald Trump. It’s summer 2017, and he’s been given the job of comms director, which he doesn’t know how to do, but he and Trump think it’ll work out because they’re both from New York. Or maybe he took it because he had “Potomac fever”, which afflicts Wall Street financiers who find themselves on the riverfront in Washington DC thinking they know how to run a country just because they’re “full of power and judgmental insight … about to fix everything”. This appointment lasts only 11 days, not even enough time to be truly tainted by Trump’s first term, though it is enough time for Scaramucci to miss the birth of his son. The account is a mea culpa soup, with the author full of regrets for his hubris, his impulsivity, his “pride, egotism and asinine stupidity”, the fact that, despite the clear-sightedness bestowed by his humble beginnings, he’d come to assume the collective biases of the rich people he hung out with. items.title: End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor review – the fightback starts here
items.summary: A sharp analysis of the damage wrought by the reckless super-rich, and a progressive toolkit for repairing it The more power the radical rightwing nationalists of our age accrue, the greater the risk that their destructive brand of politics becomes normalised. We should not, for instance, regard it as normal that the man in charge of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals casually promises “a whole civilisation will die tonight”. We should not accept that history’s first trillionaire is allowed to spread racist conspiracy theories to a hitherto unimaginable extent. We should be alarmed that, here in the UK, a party tipped to lead a potential future government is trying to cruise to power in the slipstream of this international movement. In fact, we shouldn’t just be alarmed by such developments: we should stop them and urgently repair the damage already done. But how? And what is the nature of that damage? This bold, clarifying intervention from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor provides some of the answers. “End times fascism” is their term for a convergence of interests that can broadly be understood as a response to the climate crisis. Faced with a world coming under unprecedented strain from environmental shocks and an unequal, resource-hungry economic system, today’s reactionaries are effectively saying: bring it on.
